papers.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
papers.abstract: Robot policies deployed in-the-wild should have the capability to continually learn new tasks without forgetting existing behaviors. A common method to combat such catastrophic forgetting is to train on new task data with a replay buffer of previously learned task data. Although it is common to pick this buffer randomly from all prior experiences, our work shows that a small set of these experiences contributes greatly in anchoring past performance. We call these experiences, Memory Anchors. We propose identifying Memory Anchors as areas of representation collapse between the set of old and new task data that conflict in their required actions, like manipulating a familiar object in a new manner. The old data present in this region regularizes the new task training and prevents destructive overwriting of past task knowledge, serving as this critical Memory Anchor role. Removing access to 10% of these Memory Anchors in the replay buffer leads to more than a 4.5x increase in catastrophic forgetting on the LIBERO benchmark suites. We further demonstrate that enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors can decrease worst-case forgetting in LIBERO by 63% and lead to successful continual learning of highly-conflicting tasks on a real robot.

papers.title: AnyRank: Reliable Anytime Policy Ranking via Sequential Testing
papers.abstract: Due to the high cost of hardware experiments, robot policies are predominantly evaluated by comparing their empirical performance on a limited number of hardware trials. However, finite-sample statistical uncertainty can lead to erroneous conclusions, especially when ranking multiple policies using a fixed batch of evaluation data. We propose \algname: a \emph{sequential} method for policy ranking that (i) \emph{adaptively allocates trials} to hard-to-separate policies, (ii) provides (partial) rankings at \emph{any stopping time} while bounding the probability of an incorrect ranking, and (iii) optionally \emph{exploits prior information} to prioritize hardware evaluations more efficiently using a small set of held-out hardware evaluations or rollouts in a world model. We achieve these properties through novel theoretical contributions that combine sequential and multiple-hypothesis testing. Experiments in simulation and real-world policy evaluation benchmarks show that \algname requires up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations compared to existing statistically rigorous approaches, while guarding against the incorrect rankings produced by heuristic methods used by state-of-the-art benchmarks.
